procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Additional District and Sessions Judge
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the High Court dated 30.04.2021 in Criminal RC (MD) No. 533 of 2020, which ordered further investigation.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. The Trial Judge dismissed the application filed by respondent No. 1 on 29.11.2019.
2. The first respondent challenged the order dated 29.11.2019 dismissing the petition under Section 311 Cr.P.C. before the High Court via Crl. O.P (MD) No. 18701 of 2019. The High Court dismissed this petition on 16.12.2019.
3. Respondent No. 1 filed a criminal revision before the High Court. The High Court allowed the application in the impugned order dated 30.04.2021 in Criminal RC (MD) No. 533 of 2020, ordering further investigation.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant filed a Special Leave Petition on 14.03.2022 challenging the High Court's order. On 16.08.2022, the Supreme Court issued notice and stayed the operation of the High Court's order. The Supreme Court ultimately allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment and dismissing the application for further investigation. The Supreme Court also directed that the additional charge sheet dated 02.12.2021 will not be taken on record.

directions: The judgment of the High Court dated 30.04.2021 in Criminal RC (MD) No. 533 of 2020 is set aside.

Cr. M.P. No 40/2020 in S.C. No. 61/2014 filed by the respondent no. 1 before the Court of Additional District and Sessions Judge for further investigation under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. would stand dismissed.
The additional charge sheet dated 02.12.2021 will not be taken on record.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in ordering a further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. on the facts of the case.

facts: An application for further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. was filed by the first respondent after the conclusion of evidence in the trial.
The trial court dismissed this application, holding that further investigation could not be ordered at the post-cognizance stage.
The High Court, exercising its revisional jurisdiction, overturned the trial court's decision and ordered a further investigation.

The appellant challenged the High Court's order, arguing that the application was a disguised attempt to reopen earlier proceedings, that no valid grounds were made out, and that the trial had already been delayed for over eleven years.
law: The power to order a further investigation under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. is a significant power that must be exercised sparingly, in exceptional cases, and to achieve the ends of justice.
A court must evaluate the specific facts and circumstances to determine if a further investigation is necessary to uncover the truth and deliver justice.
There must be a reasonable basis for an application for further investigation; it cannot be used for a "fishing and roving enquiry," especially after a charge-sheet has already been filed.
While the High Court has inherent powers to order further investigation, these powers must be used fairly, with circumspection, and in exceptional cases.
Denial of speedy and timely justice is detrimental to the rule of law, and courts must be vigilant against attempts to delay proceedings without valid justification.
application: The Supreme Court decided the case on its merits, finding it unnecessary to rule on the jurisdictional question of whether a court could order further investigation after the conclusion of evidence.
The Court found the High Court's direction for further investigation to be "absolutely unwarranted" on the facts.

It noted that the applicant for further investigation had not mentioned anything new in her own evidence that she was now seeking to introduce through the application, indicating a lack of reasonable basis for the request.
The Court characterized the application as a "fishing and roving enquiry" rather than a genuine effort to find truth.

The Court heavily criticized the extensive delay of over eleven years in the trial and concluded that the High Court had allowed the further investigation without providing any valid justification, which would only prolong the proceedings further.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in ordering a further investigation. The direction was found to be unwarranted based on the facts, as there was no reasonable basis for the request, and it would only contribute to the already significant delay in the trial. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and the original application for further investigation.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial court had jurisdiction to entertain an application for further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. after the conclusion of evidence.

facts: An application for further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. was filed by the first respondent after the conclusion of evidence in the trial.
The trial court dismissed the application, but the High Court allowed it, ordering further investigation.
The appellant argued before the Supreme Court that the trial court had no jurisdiction to entertain such an application at that late stage of the proceedings.
law: The legal question raised was whether a court has jurisdiction to order further investigation under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. after the trial has effectively concluded, with one side arguing that it could only be ordered until the commencement of the trial.
application: The Supreme Court explicitly stated that it would not decide the legal issue of the trial court's jurisdiction.
The Court reasoned that since it was already inclined to set aside the High Court's order based on the merits of the case, it was unnecessary to discuss and rule on the jurisdictional question.
Instead of deciding the legal point, the Court focused on whether the High Court was justified in ordering further investigation based on the specific facts and circumstances.
The Court found that the application for further investigation was a "fishing and roving enquiry," lacked a reasonable basis, and was an unwarranted attempt to delay the proceedings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not decide the issue of whether the trial court had jurisdiction to entertain the application. It explicitly deemed it "unnecessary to discuss the issue of jurisdiction" because it resolved the case on its merits, finding that the High Court's order for further investigation was factually unjustified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in ordering a further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. on the facts of the case.
appellant_arguments: The application for further investigation was a disguised attempt to reopen earlier proceedings under Section 311 of the Cr.P.C. which had already attained finality.
No sufficient grounds were presented to warrant a further investigation.
The application was intended to fill the lacunae in the prosecution's case.
The allegations of threats to witnesses were denied, noting that no such complaint had been made in the preceding seven years, even when the witnesses were examined in court.
The High Court should not have interfered with the trial court's order in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction.
Even the State had previously argued before the lower courts that the investigation had been conducted properly and a complete charge-sheet was filed.
respondent_arguments: The interest of justice is paramount and should override concerns about delays in the proceedings.
A further investigation has already been conducted in compliance with the High Court's order, and an additional charge-sheet with new facts and material has been prepared.
No prejudice would be caused to the accused, as they will be provided with the new material and given ample opportunity to present their defence.
The application was filed only after the High Court, while dismissing an earlier petition under Section 311, noted that no prayer for further investigation had been made.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial court had jurisdiction to entertain an application for further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. after the conclusion of evidence.
appellant_arguments: The trial court lacked jurisdiction to entertain an application for further investigation after charges had been framed.
A victim or complainant cannot file an application for further investigation at the post-cognizance stage.
Further investigation at such a late stage can only be initiated at the behest of the investigating agency, not the victim.
The application was filed extremely late in the trial, after the conclusion of evidence, examination of the accused under Section 313, and completion of final arguments by the defence.
respondent_arguments: The interest of justice is paramount, implying that the court should have the power to order further investigation at any stage if the facts and circumstances require it.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power to order a further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is a significant power that must be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional cases to achieve the ends of justice.
obiter: The question of whether a trial court has the jurisdiction to order a further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, after the conclusion of evidence is left undecided as the case is resolved on its merits.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's direction for a further investigation under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. was absolutely unwarranted on the facts of the case. The High Court failed to record any valid legal reasoning or apply the established principles that such a power must be exercised sparingly and in exceptional circumstances, instead justifying its order on grounds that were legally insufficient.
legal_tests_applied: The power to order further investigation is a significant power which has to be exercised sparingly and in exceptional cases and to achieve the ends of justice.
A satisfaction of want of proper, fair, impartial and effective investigation eroding its credence and reliability is the precondition for a direction for further investigation or re-investigation.

The prime concern and the endeavour of the court of law should be to secure justice on the basis of true facts which ought to be unearthed through a committed, resolved and a competent investigating agency.

If there is necessity for further investigation, the same can certainly be done as prescribed by law. The mere fact that there may be further delay in concluding the trial should not stand in the way of further investigation if that would help the court in arriving at the truth and do real and substantial as well as effective justice.
why_respondent_won: The High Court failed to provide any valid justification for its order, as it had not recorded any reason whatsoever and had not set out any legal principle which is relevant and applicable to the facts.
The High Court did not consider any of the established legal principles governing the exercise of power under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C.

The reasons cited by the High Court—that a prior Section 311 petition was denied, that a witness (PW-1) had turned hostile, and that it was a murder case—were insufficient to warrant a further investigation at such a late stage of the trial.
policy_considerations: Denial of speedy and timely justice can be disastrous to rule of law in the long term.
Even if the parties involved in a case themselves, with no valid justification attempt to delay the proceedings, the courts need to be vigilant and nip any such attempt in the bud instantly.
Any proceeding or application which prima facie lacks merit should not be instituted in a court.
Frivolous and vexatious proceedings directly impinge on the rule of law, because they add to the pendency and the consequential delay in the disposal of other cases which are crying for justice.
It is time that such frivolous and vexatious proceedings are met with due sanctions in the form of exemplary costs to dissuade parties from resorting to such tactics.
